subtopics.title: What Turns Rain into a Flood — Physical Causes

questions.question: Sixty millimetres of rain in ninety minutes floods where the same amount over a fortnight does not, because:
options: Short storms carry warmer water
Intense rain arrives faster than the soil can absorb it, so most runs straight off the surface
Rain over a fortnight evaporates before landing
Rain gauges under-read slow rain

questions.question: A cut-off low produces wide-area flooding because it:
options: Moves rapidly along the coast
Only forms in winter
Pinches off from the westerly wind belt and stalls, raining over the same catchments for days
Draws water out of rivers

questions.question: Antecedent moisture influences flooding because soil that is already saturated:
options: Converts nearly every new drop of rain into surface runoff
Absorbs more of the next storm
Cools the catchment and stops rain
Blocks water from reaching rivers

questions.question: A round, compact catchment tends to flood harder than a long thin one because it:
options: Receives more intense thunderstorms
Has steeper slopes by definition
Contains fewer rivers
Drains every corner to the outlet in roughly equal travel time, so the whole storm arrives together

questions.question: Urbanisation amplifies floods in two connected ways:
options: Cities warm the air and attract cyclones
Sealed surfaces stop infiltration, and stormwater pipes deliver runoff to rivers at speed
Urban rivers carry less sediment
City trees intercept too much rain

questions.question: A healthy wetland reduces flooding because it:
options: Evaporates most of the flood water
Diverts rivers away from towns
Spreads and stores an arriving surge, then releases it slowly over weeks
Raises the riverbed with silt

questions.question: Beyond faster runoff, deforestation and overgrazing worsen later floods because:
options: Eroded sediment settles on riverbeds and dam floors, raising channels and shrinking storage
Bare soil attracts cut-off lows
Livestock drink from the rivers
Grass roots block stormwater drains

questions.question: In South Africa, exposure to flooding maps onto poverty because:
options: Storms target dense settlements
Wealthy suburbs are built below the flood line
Municipal drains only serve farms
The unclaimed land left for those with the fewest choices is so often the flood-prone land beside rivers

subtopics.title: The Flood Hydrograph, Described in Words

questions.question: A flood hydrograph plots:
options: Rainfall against evaporation
River depth against channel width
Time on the horizontal axis against discharge in cumecs on the vertical axis
Catchment area against rainfall total

questions.question: Base flow is supplied by:
options: Groundwater seeping steadily from saturated ground into the channel
The first surface runoff of a storm
Water released from upstream dams
Rain falling directly onto the river

questions.question: Lag time is defined as the interval between:
options: The start of the rain and the start of the rising limb
The heaviest rainfall and peak discharge
Peak discharge and the return to base flow
Two successive flood peaks

questions.question: The falling limb descends more gently than the rising limb climbed because:
options: Rivers flow slower downhill after storms
The gauge loses accuracy at high flows
Evaporation removes the flood water gradually
The late-arriving water travels by slower routes — through the soil and from the catchment's far edges

subtopics.title: Reading Hydrographs — Urban Against Rural, Flash Against Regional

questions.question: After a catchment is urbanised, the same storm produces a hydrograph with:
options: A shorter lag, a higher narrower peak and steeper limbs
A longer lag and a broader peak
A stronger base flow between storms
No measurable change

questions.question: The rural grassland catchment keeps a healthy base flow between storms because:
options: Its stormwater pipes recycle water
Rain falls more often over grassland
Groundwater recharged during storms keeps paying into the channel
Wetlands pump water upstream

questions.question: The Jukskei flood of December 2022 was a flash flood because:
options: It lasted several weeks across Gauteng
It was caused by a tropical cyclone at the coast
A dam wall failed upstream of Alexandra
An intense storm on a heavily sealed urban catchment raised the river within minutes, leaving no time for warning

questions.question: The Natal floods of September 1987 count as a regional flood because:
options: They peaked within minutes in one valley
A stalled cut-off low rained for days over a wide area, keeping many rivers high across the province
Only one river was affected
They caused no damage to infrastructure

questions.question: In the bucket experiment, the paved driveway stands for:
options: Every surface that refuses to drink — bare rock, baked or saturated soil, and the sealed city
A wetland at the bottom of a valley
Deep sandy soil under grass
A catchment with a long lag time

questions.question: A thoroughly soaked lawn sheds the next bucket like paving because:
options: Wet grass becomes waterproof
The water bounces off the grass blades
Saturated soil has no storage left, so new water runs off as if the ground were sealed
Lawns slope more steeply when wet

questions.question: The sprinkler and the pressure washer deliver the same litres, but only the pressure washer floods the lawn. The lesson is:
options: Total rainfall matters more than anything
The rate at which water arrives matters more than the total — intensity beats total
Lawns can absorb unlimited water
Pressure washers use warmer water

questions.question: Rivers keep murmuring through the dry season because:
options: Dew refills the channel each night
Rain always falls somewhere upstream
The sea pushes water inland
Base flow — groundwater seeping out of the earth — keeps feeding the channel

questions.question: The river's sound does not change the moment the rain starts because:
options: Water landing on distant slopes still needs travel time to reach the gauge — the lag time
Rain falls silently on water
The channel empties before it fills
Base flow blocks the new water

questions.question: The three questions that interpret any hydrograph are:
options: How wide, how muddy, how cold
Which river, which season, which province
How high the peak, how soon after the rain, how steep the climb
How long, how deep, how salty

questions.question: After the storm the river settles at a slightly fuller murmur than before because:
options: The channel widened during the flood
The soaked ground keeps topping the channel up, so base flow sits a little higher
Stormwater pipes discharge for weeks
The gauge recalibrates after floods

subtopics.title: The Jukskei and the Natal Floods — Lessons From Real Floods

questions.question: The Jukskei answers a Highveld storm almost immediately because its catchment:
options: Lies on steep mountain slopes
Has been stripped by overgrazing
Is fed by melting snow
Is sealed under the roofs, roads and paving of northern Johannesburg, all plumbed toward the channel

questions.question: In September 1987, Natal's rivers rose and stayed up for days because:
options: A stalled cut-off low delivered several hundred millimetres onto ground already soaked
A single thunderstorm struck one valley
Dams released water simultaneously
High tides blocked the river mouths

questions.question: Placed side by side, the two events illustrate:
options: Two regional floods of equal duration
Two flash floods in rural catchments
The Jukskei as the sharp flash-flood spike and Natal 1987 as the broad, sustained regional flood
Natal 1987 as the flash flood and the Jukskei as the regional flood

questions.question: Every remedy the two disasters teach works by:
options: Increasing peak discharge safely
Lengthening the lag or lowering the peak — protecting wetlands, unsealing ground, clearing drains, keeping homes off floodplains, warning faster than the water
Preventing rain over cities
Straightening river channels everywhere
